Human anatomy is the scientific study of the body's structure—its bones, muscles, organs, and systems—and how these components are organized and interrelated. Emerging from ancient dissection practices and formalized during the Renaissance through systematic observation and artistic representation, anatomy became foundational to medicine, art, and scientific understanding. The discipline bridges empirical observation with artistic and medical application, making it central to both the development of modern medicine and the Renaissance artistic revolution's pursuit of naturalistic representation.

Ancient civilizations including Egypt, Greece, and Rome practiced dissection and developed early anatomical understanding. Galen in the second century CE conducted animal dissections and inferred human anatomy, establishing an authority that dominated Western medicine for over thirteen hundred years despite numerous inaccuracies. Renaissance anatomists challenged Galen's legacy through systematic human dissection. Andreas Vesalius's De Humani Corporis Fabrica, published in 1543, corrected Galenic errors through meticulous observation and created beautifully illustrated anatomical images that merged science and art.

Leonardo da Vinci conducted dozens of human dissections and produced extraordinarily accurate anatomical drawings that captured muscle structure, organ placement, and skeletal mechanics. His Vitruvian Man symbolized the Renaissance fusion of art and anatomical knowledge. The development of the microscope in the seventeenth century revealed microscopic structures invisible to the naked eye. Anton van Leeuwenhoek and Robert Hooke discovered cells, fundamentally expanding anatomical understanding. Systematic classification of anatomical structures emerged during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, establishing standardized terminology that enabled precise communication among medical professionals and supported the development of pathology and surgical technique.

Comparative anatomy—studying anatomical structures across animal species—provided evidence for evolutionary relationships. Darwin and other naturalists used anatomical homologies to argue for common descent among organisms. Modern anatomy integrates multiple scales of analysis from gross anatomy to tissue structure to cellular and molecular anatomy. Imaging technologies including X-ray, CT, and MRI now enable three-dimensional visualization of living bodies. Artistic anatomy remains central to figure drawing and sculpture, enabling artists to depict convincing human forms and movement.
